name: pulse-compare-threaded-vs-event-loop
notes:
Flip 'server profile' live: threaded (bounded workers, real admission control) vs event-loop (unlimited workers, node.js-style) against the same 5x pulse (210rps -> 1050rps over 5s, held 15s, back down over 5s -- shorter than the 30s boot time, so no capacity added mid-pulse can help). Per-request CPU time and I/O wait are now exponential (shifted-exp, near-zero floor + an exponential tail: cpuTimeMs mean ~16ms, ioWaitMs mean ~51ms) instead of fixed, so service time has real variance -- the same shape burstiness a real fleet sees from cache misses or GC pauses. Base load is sized so 4 instances is the right starting point (`initialInstances: 4`, both variants start there identically).

Threaded's worker count is deliberately tuned to 15 with queueSlots at 0 (reject immediately once all 15 are busy -- no extra waiting room) for a specific reason: on 4 cores, once cpu time has real variance, MORE workers doesn't mean LESS latency -- cpuPool's queue is sized to `workers`, so a bigger worker pool just lets more admitted requests pile up waiting for the same 4 cores, and latency-of-the-admitted RISES (measured: workers=30 -> p95 ~211ms; workers=300 -> p95 ~870-1000ms, WORSE). Shrinking workers instead sheds the overflow at the door -- the ones that get in never queue behind ones that don't. Measured (seeds 1-5): threaded holds p95 latency at ~185-200ms throughout -- baseline, ramp, hold, and recovery are all indistinguishable -- for the cost of ~1.7-1.8% rejected, entirely inside the pulse window.

Event-loop (unlimited workers, 1 core, same exponential service time, same 210rps base) shows 0% errors -- nothing is ever rejected -- but the same pulse produces a mean latency spike of ~10-11.5s and a p95 spike of ~13-14.4s, both peaking just after the pulse itself ends, before the (up to 20-instance) scale-out and boot delay catch up. Zero rejections looks like success on an error-rate dashboard; it isn't. Same load, same variance, same instance count at the moment the pulse lands -- the only variable is whether the unit can say no. Threaded's tuned worker count turns 'too much load' into a small, fast, visible rejection rate. Unlimited workers turn it into an invisible, order-of-magnitude latency event.
